title: How can African nations benefit from their mineral resources?
gist: A Benchmark recap of its Giga Africa event in Marrakesh. It argues that Africa has become strategically significant as Europe and North America diversify away from China-centric battery supply chains, and that African states are using raw-mineral export bans to force domestic refining. A key tension: Chinese firms are likely to build the near-term processing capacity, while African miners such as Buenassa want local ownership with foreign partners only in support.

insights.claim: Africa has rapidly grown from a small player into a strategically significant part of the global battery supply chain, as Europe and North America look to diversify away from China-centric supply chains.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Western policy that rewards non-China supply can push capital toward African mining and processing.
insights.quote: Africa has rapidly grown from a small player in the global battery supply chain to a strategically significant one
insights.locator: In recent years, Africa has rapidly

insights.claim: Benchmark CEO Andrew Miller argued that Africa will be very important for supplying the fastest-growing battery demand channels in Europe and North America.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Western EV and battery makers will increasingly sign offtake deals with African projects.
insights.quote: When we think about supplying those fastest demand growth channels in Europe and North America, Africa is going to be incredibly important in that mix.

insights.claim: Africa holds every mineral a battery needs: lithium in Zimbabwe, copper and cobalt in the DRC, nickel and copper in Zambia, manganese in South Africa, phosphates in Morocco and graphite in Mozambique.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Because the continent covers the full bill of materials, a regionally integrated cell supply chain is at least possible in theory.
insights.locator: How is Africa positioned for the battery industry?

insights.claim: Zimbabwe's Ministry of Mines (Chief Director Leon Godza) is calling on African countries to collaborate through a cross-border economic zone, so that minerals are eventually turned into cathode, anode and cells within Africa.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: If a cross-border zone forms, it could change where cathode and anode plants get built, though doing it across several countries is hard.
insights.quote: The important thing is to encourage collaboration between the cross-border economic zone for battery and electric vehicle production.

insights.claim: Historically, much of the value from Africa's natural resources has been captured outside the region, even though investment from China, North America and Europe is vital for growth.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: This history explains why resource nationalism is rising, which increases policy risk for foreign-owned miners.
insights.quote: historically much of the value from Africa’s natural resources has been captured outside of the region
insights.locator: Will African nations benefit from this?

insights.claim: Khalid Hammouch of Managem framed the battery value chain as controlled by whoever owns refining and transformation, not by whoever holds reserves.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Midstream refiners deserve a premium over pure reserve holders, which favours integrated African players such as Managem.
insights.quote: Whoever controls the transformation step controls the value chain.

insights.claim: Over the last few years, many African countries have banned or controlled raw-mineral exports to encourage domestic refining capacity.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Export bans can tighten global concentrate supply and force miners to spend capex on in-country processing.
insights.quote: banning or controlling the export of raw minerals to incentivise the build-out of domestic refining capacity
insights.locator: To this end, many African countries

insights.claim: In the short term, Benchmark expects African processing capacity to be built mainly by foreign companies, especially Chinese ones, because of their deep expertise in mineral refining.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Export bans meant to diversify away from China may end up producing Chinese-owned refining in Africa, which could clash with Western foreign-entity-of-concern rules.
insights.quote: it is likely that processing capabilities will be developed by foreign entities, especially Chinese companies
insights.locator: In the short term, it is

insights.claim: Eddy Kioni, CEO of DRC miner Buenassa, argued that Congolese players should own and run processing themselves, with foreign partners in a supporting role rather than owning the capacity.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Local-ownership demands point to tighter terms for foreign investors in DRC processing joint ventures.
insights.quote: It is not only about processing locally; it is [about] processing by locals with support from foreign partners.
